title: Fewest coins for an amount
prompt:
coins holds distinct positive denominations, each available in unlimited supply. Return the fewest coins that add up exactly to amount, or -1 if it cannot be made.

- 1 to 12 denominations between 1 and 10,000; 0 <= amount <= 10,000.
- Greedy (always take the largest coin) is not always optimal.
hints: Why does taking the biggest coin first fail for coins [1, 3, 4] and amount 6?
Let best[a] be the fewest coins for amount a. The last coin used is some c, leaving a - c.
best[0] = 0; best[a] = 1 + min(best[a - c]) over coins c <= a with best[a - c] reachable. Fill a from 1 to amount.

solution.explanation: Any optimal way to make a ends with some coin c, and the rest must be an optimal way to make a - c (optimal substructure). Computing best[] bottom-up from 0 means every smaller amount is ready when it is needed. Unreachable amounts stay at infinity.

complexity.notes: k is the number of denominations. BFS over amounts gives the same answer, since every coin adds exactly one to the count.

followUps: Count the number of distinct ways to make the amount instead. Why does loop order now matter?
